title: Parental psychological problems were associated with higher screen time and the use of mature-rated media in children
authors: Pulkki-Råback L, Barnes JD, Elovainio M, Hakulinen C, Sourander A, Tremblay MS, Guerrero MD

primary_models.name: Multilevel general linear model of child social media minutes/day on presence of parental psychological problem, basic adjustments (Model 1)
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3, 'Social media' columns, 'Model 1: basic adjustments' rows (p. 830); described in Results p. 829 ('There were no significant associations between parental psychological problems and children's use of social media') and Discussion p. 831.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD baseline visit (2016-2018). Parent-reported psychopathology (IV) and child-reported screen time (DV) measured at the same visit. One observation per child. Phone/SM is the DV here: the predictor is a binary indicator of clinically significant parental psychological problems and the outcome is the child's daily minutes of social media. Each parental problem scale (externalising, internalising, total) is entered as the predictor in a separate model, with the reference group being children whose parent does not have that problem.
primary_models.sample: ABCD baseline data released in 2019 (NDA DOI 10.15154/1524631), N = 11,875 enrolled; 10,650 participants with complete data on study variables. 5112 girls and 5538 boys, mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6). Child-identified ethnicity: Black n = 1480, Asian n = 215, White n = 5843, Hispanic n = 1746, Multiracial n = 1366. Main caregiver was the mother for 85% and father/other for 15%. 16.7% of children had a psychological problem (CBCL). Parental problem prevalence (Table 1): externalising 935 (8.8%), internalising 1425 (13.4%), total problems 446 (4.2%).
primary_models.iv: Presence of a clinically significant parental psychological problem from the Adult Self-Report (ASR, 123 items, 0/1/2 response), completed by the main caregiver. Three broadband scales are used: externalising, internalising and total problems. Raw scores were converted to gender-normed T-scores and dichotomised at T >= 65 (clinically significant problem = 1) vs T < 65 (= 0). Prevalence: externalising 8.8%, internalising 13.4%, total 4.2% (Table 1, p. 828).
primary_models.dv: Child-reported daily minutes of social media use from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey. The social media item covers visiting social networking sites such as Twitter or Instagram; the paper's methods list texting and video chat as separate questionnaire activities, and the paper does not state explicitly whether they were folded into the 'social media' category. Responses on a 7-point scale (none, <30 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, >=4 h) for a typical weekday and weekend day; daily minutes computed as (weekday minutes x 5 + weekend minutes x 2)/7. Mean 30.8 (SD 66.14) min/day in the full sample; girls 35.7 (69.9), boys 26.2 (62.1) (Table 1, p. 828). 43% of children reported no social media use.

covariates.name: Presence of child psychological problem
covariates.detail: Child Behaviour Checklist, >95th percentile (borderline clinical) on each scale; 1778 (16.7%) children

primary_models.equation: SM_minutes[i,site] = b0 + b1*ParentProblem[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4*ethnicity + b5*family_income + b6*main_caregiver + b7*child_psych_problem + u_site + e[i], fitted separately with ParentProblem = externalising, internalising, or total problems (each coded 1 = T >= 65 vs 0 = T < 65). b1 is the adjusted difference in daily social media minutes between children of parents with vs without the problem.
primary_models.estimation: Multilevel general linear model with a random intercept for study site; coefficients are raw (unstandardised) minutes/day. Analyses conducted in RStudio 1.1.463. No survey weights reported. No multiple-comparison correction; significance flagged at p < 0.05 and p < 0.01. Table 3 column headers for the non-TV activities are printed as 'OR', but the table title and footnotes identify these as multilevel general linear model coefficients in minutes per day (the same as the TV 'Coeff.' column). Gender interaction terms (parental problem x child gender) were tested; results reported in Table S2 (not bundled in the PDF). A second step (Model 2) additionally adjusted for family conflict (extracted as M2). An additional logistic regression on any vs no social media use found no association (p-values 0.201 to 0.786; ORs not printed).

d_transformation.conversion_formula: Dichotomous IV -> continuous DV: d = (adjusted M1 - M0) / SD_pooled = B / SD_DV, using the full-sample SD of social media minutes/day (66.14) as an approximation of the pooled within-group SD. CI endpoints converted the same way (B_lo / SD_DV, B_hi / SD_DV).
d_transformation.contrast_type: Parent with clinically significant problem (ASR T >= 65) vs parent without the problem
d_transformation.notes: SD_DV = 66.14 min/day from Table 1 (p. 828, 'All (n = 10650)' column; printed with two decimals while other rows use one). The pooled within-group SD is not reported, so the total-sample SD is used; with exposure prevalence of 4-13% the difference should be small. SD_IV is not needed for this contrast. The authors themselves report Cohen's d of 0.09-0.10 for Table 2 total screen time results, not for social media. The DV is right-skewed (43% report zero social media), so d based on SD of a skewed outcome should be read with caution. This d (group difference / SD) is not directly comparable to per-1-SD-of-IV d values from continuous-IV papers.

extraction_flags: 1) Which specification to anchor on is unclear. The abstract quotes Model 1 numbers (basic adjustments), and the text says nothing changed after adding family conflict (Model 2). I extracted both as M1 and M2. A coder should strike whichever one the review does not want. 2) Phone/SM is the DV here: parental ASR problem (binary, T >= 65) predicts the child's social media minutes per day. 3) In Table 3, the Video/youtube, Video games and Social media columns are headed 'OR', but the title and the scale of the values show they are linear-model coefficients in minutes per day. I coded them as B. 4) No p-values are printed for the social media cells. They have no asterisk, so I set them to p null and sig false. 5) Paper-wide social media prevalence is 43% non-users and Table 1's SD is printed as '66.14', with two decimals where every other row has one. Please check the SD_DV, which comes from Table 1. Since the pooled within-group SD is not reported, d = B/66.14 is an approximation, and the outcome is highly skewed. 6) The paper does not say clearly whether the 'social media' category includes texting and video chat or only social networking sites. 7) The logistic model for any vs no social media use gives only a p-value range, with no ORs. The supplementary Tables S2-S4 are not in the PDF, so these are listed under excluded models.json
